opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. For me, it really comes down to where I think the bottleneck in AI is going to be over the next several years.

Everyone talks about models, and models matter enormously. But a model is only as useful as your ability to serve it efficiently, reliably, and cheaply. When we started working on SGLang and ideas like RadixAttention back in the research days, what struck us was how much performance was being left on the table. The same model, on the same hardware, could be several times faster or cheaper depending on how you scheduled requests, reused the KV cache, and handled structured outputs or multi-turn agent workloads. That gap isn't a detail. It decides whether a product is economically viable at all.

So being infra-first is a deliberate bet. Applications will come and go, and model architectures will keep changing, but every one of them needs a strong runtime underneath. If we do our job well, we make everyone above us faster: the labs training and serving frontier models, the startups building agents, the enterprises running open models on their own hardware.

There's also a personal side. I came up through systems research, and I've always believed the most leverage comes from building foundations other people can build on. Open source has been central to that. SGLang grew because a large community of contributors and users pushed it in directions we never would have found alone. Starting RadixArk as an infrastructure company lets us keep investing in that core seriously, with a team that can work on the hard problems full-time: scheduling, memory management, new hardware, large-scale distributed inference, and increasingly the overlap between inference and training, like reinforcement learning rollouts.

And honestly, infrastructure is where trust gets built. People only run their production workloads on something they believe will be there, will be fast, and will keep improving. I want RadixArk to be that layer people don't have to worry about, so they can put their energy into what they're actually trying to build.

r002.rationale: It presents the runtime as a foundation others build on and describes RadixArk as a company investing in that infrastructure layer as a core offering.

r003.rationale: The response mentions trust and reducing users’ worries, but does not argue that infrastructure appeals to human nature.

r004.rationale: It says that doing the job well makes everyone above RadixArk faster, naming labs, startups, and enterprises as examples.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. For me it comes down to where the real leverage is. Over the past few years I spent most of my time on SGLang, and what I kept seeing is that model progress gets a lot of the attention, but the thing that actually decides whether a model is usable at scale is the serving layer underneath it. Latency, throughput, cost per token, how well you handle long shared prefixes, how you schedule across thousands of GPUs. Those problems are deep, they're unglamorous, and they don't go away when the next model comes out. If anything they get harder.

So when we started RadixArk, I didn't want to be a company that trains a model and then treats infrastructure as an afterthought. I wanted infrastructure to be the product and the identity. The name itself comes from the radix tree we use for prefix caching in SGLang. That's a signal to ourselves about what we care about.

There's also an open-source philosophy behind it. SGLang grew because a lot of people, from universities to big labs, contributed and ran it in production, and that feedback loop made the system much better than any one team could have. Being infra-first lets us keep that core open while building the things on top that companies actually need to run it reliably. I think that's a more honest and more durable way to build a company in this space than chasing whichever benchmark is hot this quarter.

And personally, I just enjoy this layer. Making a system go from a thousand tokens per second to ten thousand on the same hardware is the kind of problem I like waking up to.

astra-6.text:
For me, it comes down to the gap between what AI models can do and what people can actually afford to deploy. A model can be incredibly capable, but if running it is too expensive, too slow, or unreliable, that capability doesn’t translate into a useful product.

That’s why I think it’s important to build RadixArk with infrastructure at the center. The decisions you make early—how you use compute, how you handle different workloads, how you balance latency and throughput—shape what developers can build on top. Those aren’t things you can always fix by adding another layer later.

And the impact is broad. If we make the underlying infrastructure more efficient and easier to use, we’re helping many teams experiment and bring products to users. That’s the part that’s exciting to me: making more of what’s possible with AI practical.

r002.rationale: It says infrastructure should be at the center of RadixArk’s work, but does not present infrastructure itself as a product.

r003.rationale: The response does not connect infrastructure to human nature.

r004.rationale: It explains that early infrastructure decisions shape what developers can build on top, describing effects that flow upward through the technology stack.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, it starts with the idea that infrastructure determines what people can actually build. You can have a very capable model, but if serving it is too expensive, too slow, or too difficult to operate, that capability doesn’t translate into a useful product.

So with RadixArk, we want to work on that foundation: making inference more efficient, reliable, and accessible. And that requires treating infrastructure as the core product. You have to think about the whole system—how the software interacts with the hardware, how workloads are scheduled, and what developers experience when they deploy something.

What excites me is the multiplier effect. If we improve that foundation, we can help many different teams build better applications. That’s why being infra-first matters to me.
